parts:
Hi all,

I'm a new NIMBLE user (coming from Stan) and am trying to reproduce one of the models from this paper (specifically model K-L3), which uses a Chinese Restaurant Process to cluster verbs into classes, based on the distribution estimated from a Dirichlet-multinomial model of how often each verb occurs in each of two alternating constructions. I believe I have constructed this model correctly and am using a small sample of data reported in the above paper to verify this, but unfortunately each time I run the MCMC sampling, the R session aborts. I have tried compiling the model and checking to ensure that I'm not getting infinite/NaN/NA values for the log probabilities, which is not the case. I have a hunch that it may be related to the initial values I set for the parameters, but I'm really at quite a loss and would appreciate any help, advice, or just a second set of eyes on my code in case I'm missing another problem.

k.l3_model <- nimbleCode({
  z[1:N] ~ dCRP(conc = gamma, size = N)
 
  for(c in 1:K) {
    lambda[c] ~ dexp(1.0)
    alpha[c] ~ dexp(lambda[c])
    mu[c] ~ dexp(1.0)
   
    mu_vec[c,1:2] <- rep(mu[c], times=2)
   
    beta[c,1:2] ~ ddirch(mu_vec[c,1:2])
  }
 
  for (i in 1:N) {
    ab[i,1:2] <- alpha[z[i]]*beta[z[i],1:2]
    theta[i,1:2] ~ ddirch(ab[i,1:2])
    y[i,1:2] ~ dmulti(prob=theta[i,1:2], size=n_i[i])
  }
})

Here are the data I'm using:
ptw_e0 <- tribble(
  # y = vector with form DOD, PD
  ~v, ~verb, ~dod, ~pd, ~y,
  1, "read", 1,  1, mvbind(1,1),
  2, "give", 2,  1, mvbind(2,1),
  3, "show", 2,  1, mvbind(2,1)
) %>% mutate(n_i = rowSums(across(c(dod, pd))))

And here is the initialization, compilation, and sampling code:
exp2_consts <- list(N = nrow(ptw_e0),
                    K = 3,
                    gamma = 1)
exp2_data <- list(y = ptw_e0$y,

       z = rep(1, 3))
chain1.inits$alpha <- rep(rexp(n=1, rate=chain1.inits$lambda), 3)
chain1.inits$mu_vec <- matrix(rep(chain1.inits$mu[1], 6), nrow = 3, ncol = 2)
chain1.inits$beta <-  matrix(rep(brms::rdirichlet(n=1, alpha=rep(chain1.inits$mu[1], 2)), 3), nrow = 3, ncol = 2, byrow=TRUE)
chain1.inits$theta <- matrix(rep(brms::rdirichlet(n=1, alpha=chain1.inits$alpha[1]*chain1.inits$beta[1,]), 3), nrow = 3, ncol = 2, byrow=TRUE)

chain2.inits <- list(lambda = rep(rexp(n=1, rate=1), 3),
       mu = rep(rexp(n=1, rate=1), 3),
       z = rep(1, 3))
chain2.inits$alpha <- rep(rexp(n=1, rate=chain2.inits$lambda), 3)
chain2.inits$mu_vec <- matrix(rep(chain2.inits$mu[1], 6), nrow = 3, ncol = 2)
chain2.inits$beta <-  matrix(rep(brms::rdirichlet(n=1, alpha=rep(chain2.inits$mu[1], 2)), 3), nrow = 3, ncol = 2, byrow=TRUE)
chain2.inits$theta <- matrix(rep(brms::rdirichlet(n=1, alpha=chain2.inits$beta[1,]), 3), nrow = 3, ncol = 2, byrow=TRUE)

chain3.inits <- list(lambda = rep(rexp(n=1, rate=1), 3),
       mu = rep(rexp(n=1, rate=1), 3),
       z = rep(1, 3))
chain3.inits$alpha <- rep(rexp(n=1, rate=chain3.inits$lambda), 3)
chain3.inits$mu_vec <- matrix(rep(chain3.inits$mu[1], 6), nrow = 3, ncol = 2)
chain3.inits$beta <-  matrix(rep(brms::rdirichlet(n=1, alpha=rep(chain3.inits$mu[1], 2)), 3), nrow = 3, ncol = 2, byrow=TRUE)
chain3.inits$theta <- matrix(rep(brms::rdirichlet(n=1, alpha=chain3.inits$beta[1,]), 3), nrow = 3, ncol = 2, byrow=TRUE)

chain4.inits <- list(lambda = rep(rexp(n=1, rate=1), 3),
       mu = rep(rexp(n=1, rate=1), 3),
       z = rep(1, 3))
chain4.inits$alpha <- rep(rexp(n=1, rate=chain4.inits$lambda), 3)
chain4.inits$mu_vec <- matrix(rep(chain4.inits$mu[1], 6), nrow = 3, ncol = 2)
chain4.inits$beta <-  matrix(rep(brms::rdirichlet(n=1, alpha=rep(chain4.inits$mu[1], 2)), 3), nrow = 3, ncol = 2, byrow=TRUE)
chain4.inits$theta <- matrix(rep(brms::rdirichlet(n=1, alpha=chain4.inits$beta[1,]), 3), nrow = 3, ncol = 2, byrow=TRUE)

exp2_inits <- c(chain1.inits, chain2.inits, chain3.inits, chain4.inits)

exp2_mod <- nimbleModel(code=k.l3_model, constants = exp2_consts, data = exp2_data, inits = exp2_inits)
compiledMod <- compileNimble(exp2_mod)

params.to.save <- c("z", "theta")

n.iter <- 10000
n.burnin <- 5000
n.chains <- 4

nimbleMCMC(model=compiledMod,
           monitors = params.to.save,
           nchains = n.chains,
           niter = n.iter,
           nburnin = n.burnin,
           summary = TRUE)

Thank you so much!

--
Brennan Gonering

parts:
Hi Brennan,

It looks like this is occurring because, for the model structure and small dataset in the example, it's possible to get values in the theta and beta vectors that are exactly 0 from numerical underflow. 

The zero values in `theta` tend to happen when the `ab` values are much smaller than 1. The values of exact 0 cause the CRP sampling, which calculates the log probability density for a value of z conditional on theta, to have Infinity values when it tries to sample a new value of z, and that causes the error because we didn't anticipate the Infinity values could occur.  

The zero values in `beta` occur in the CRP sampling when attempting to create a new cluster by sampling from the prior for `beta`, and tend to happen when the `mu` values are much smaller than 1. The exact 0 value ends up causing a NaN value in the CRP sampling, which causes an error.

I'm a bit surprised this hasn't come up before, but it may be that the size of the dataset and the specific priors combine to give a somewhat unusual situation.

I've added a check that tries to handle the numerical issues more robustly, but I haven't tested it thoroughly yet.

Would you be up for installing nimble from GitHub from a new branch in which I've made these changes and seeing if it works for your use case(s)?

remotes::install_github("nimble-dev/nimble", ref = "crp_underflow", subdir = "packages/nimble")

-chris

On Mon, Oct 21, 2024 at 9:40 AM Chris Paciorek <paci...@stat.berkeley.edu> wrote:
Hi Brennan,

It looks like this is occurring because, for the model structure and small dataset in the example, it's possible to get values in the theta and beta vectors that are exactly 0 from numerical underflow. 

The zero values in `theta` tend to happen when the `ab` values are much smaller than 1. The values of exact 0 cause the CRP sampling, which calculates the log probability density for a value of z conditional on theta, to have Infinity values when it tries to sample a new value of z, and that causes the error because we didn't anticipate the Infinity values could occur.  

The zero values in `beta` occur in the CRP sampling when attempting to create a new cluster by sampling from the prior for `beta`, and tend to happen when the `mu` values are much smaller than 1. The exact 0 value ends up causing a NaN value in the CRP sampling, which causes an error.

I'm a bit surprised this hasn't come up before, but it may be that the size of the dataset and the specific priors combine to give a somewhat unusual situation.

I've added a check that tries to handle the numerical issues more robustly, but I haven't tested it thoroughly yet.

hi Brennan,

Thanks for the follow up and the additional testing.

It looks like there is another related, but distinct, numerical issue that can come up in this case. What I am seeing is that when one of the two `ab[i,1:2]` values gets close to zero, numerical underflow can cause a sampled value of `theta[i,1:2]` (from its conjugate Dirichlet distribution) to be exactly (1,0) (or (0,1)). Then if that `theta[i,1:2]` is the only member of its cluster, when the CRP sampling goes to sample a new value for `z[i]`, it's possible that the log probability density value for `theta[i,1:2]` under the other clusters are all -Inf. And using the non-conjugate CRP sampler to sample `alpha[i]` and `beta[i,1:2]` values for a new cluster will generally give values that also have -Inf for the log probability density value for `theta[i,1:2]`. At that point, the CRP sampler is trying to decide between the various possible new values for `z[i]` with all the log probabilities being -Inf and the crash occurs.

This is a tricky situation. We can of course (and will at a minimum in our upcoming release) error trap this and produce an error message rather than a crash.

However, I am not seeing a good way around the numerical problems. It's not clear to me there is a way to sample `z[i]` when `theta[i,1:2]` is (1,0) in a way that retains the validity of the MCMC sampling (i.e., I don't think sampling uniformly from the possible `z[i]` values is correct). And I don't see a reasonable way to avoid getting exact (1,0) values in the conjugate sampling of `theta[i,1:2]`.

For your case, one possible work-around (if you will generally have only two elements of theta) is that you could specify theta[i] using a beta distribution and, as needed, use truncation to ensure it never is sampled as exactly 0 or 1:

theta[i] ~ T(dbeta(ab[i,1],ab[i,2]), .001, .999)

You could also think about using the stickbreaking representation rather than the CRP.  That might avoid the issue. Or it seems that in the paper you reference, they used some other sampling strategies based on drawing from the prior.

I will try to think more about this to see if there is a better numerical solution on our end.

-chris

On Mon, Oct 28, 2024 at 9:35 AM Chris Paciorek <paci...@stat.berkeley.edu> wrote:
hi Brennan,

Thanks for the follow up and the additional testing.

It looks like there is another related, but distinct, numerical issue that can come up in this case. What I am seeing is that when one of the two `ab[i,1:2]` values gets close to zero, numerical underflow can cause a sampled value of `theta[i,1:2]` (from its conjugate Dirichlet distribution) to be exactly (1,0) (or (0,1)). Then if that `theta[i,1:2]` is the only member of its cluster, when the CRP sampling goes to sample a new value for `z[i]`, it's possible that the log probability density value for `theta[i,1:2]` under the other clusters are all -Inf. And using the non-conjugate CRP sampler to sample `alpha[i]` and `beta[i,1:2]` values for a new cluster will generally give values that also have -Inf for the log probability density value for `theta[i,1:2]`. At that point, the CRP sampler is trying to decide between the various possible new values for `z[i]` with all the log probabilities being -Inf and the crash occurs.

This is a tricky situation. We can of course (and will at a minimum in our upcoming release) error trap this and produce an error message rather than a crash.

However, I am not seeing a good way around the numerical problems. It's not clear to me there is a way to sample `z[i]` when `theta[i,1:2]` is (1,0) in a way that retains the validity of the MCMC sampling (i.e., I don't think sampling uniformly from the possible `z[i]` values is correct). And I don't see a reasonable way to avoid getting exact (1,0) values in the conjugate sampling of `theta[i,1:2]`.

For your case, one possible work-around (if you will generally have only two elements of theta) is that you could specify theta[i] using a beta distribution and, as needed, use truncation to ensure it never is sampled as exactly 0 or 1:

theta[i] ~ T(dbeta(ab[i,1],ab[i,2]), .001, .999)

You could also think about using the stickbreaking representation rather than the CRP.  That might avoid the issue. Or it seems that in the paper you reference, they used some other sampling strategies based on drawing from the prior.

I will try to think more about this to see if there is a better numerical solution on our end.

-chris

Hi Brennan,

It looks like this is occurring because, for the model structure and small dataset in the example, it's possible to get values in the theta and beta vectors that are exactly 0 from numerical underflow. 

The zero values in `theta` tend to happen when the `ab` values are much smaller than 1. The values of exact 0 cause the CRP sampling, which calculates the log probability density for a value of z conditional on theta, to have Infinity values when it tries to sample a new value of z, and that causes the error because we didn't anticipate the Infinity values could occur.  

The zero values in `beta` occur in the CRP sampling when attempting to create a new cluster by sampling from the prior for `beta`, and tend to happen when the `mu` values are much smaller than 1. The exact 0 value ends up causing a NaN value in the CRP sampling, which causes an error.

I'm a bit surprised this hasn't come up before, but it may be that the size of the dataset and the specific priors combine to give a somewhat unusual situation.

I've added a check that tries to handle the numerical issues more robustly, but I haven't tested it thoroughly yet.

parts:
Hi Brennan,

I took another look at this. It's been a bit hard to keep track of all the details here, so the following may be incomplete, but it's my current understanding:

1) Be careful about your initial values for theta. If you draw those from a beta or Dirichlet when you have a value of alpha near 0 (e.g., resulting in values of `ab` of, say, (0.1, 0.1)), it's very easy to get initial theta values that are very, very close to 0 and of exactly 1.0. These can then cause sampling issues. I suggesting initializing the theta values so they are somewhere in (0.05, 0.95) and not close to 0 or 1.
2) I think my suggestion to use truncation is not helpful as that can itself cause numerical issues when we normalize the truncated density based on using the distribution's CDF. So I suggest avoiding that. 
3) I believe that if you re-install nimble from the `crp_underflow` branch, you will no longer get crashes. I tested this with having the `beta` parameter values either from a Beta or a Dirichlet and the `theta` parameter values from a Beta, and the MCMC seemed to run. Mixing is not necessarily good, though I didn't look at it carefully. 
4) Using the Dirichlet for both `beta` and `theta` should now run. However you'll see warnings about "values of infinity for the log probability density corresponding to multiple potential cluster memberships". This occurs when sampling `z[i]` when the chain has a `theta[i,1:2]` value in which one value is exactly 1 and the other is exactly 0 or very close to 0. In the CRP sampling, when the `ab[i,1:2]` values are sufficiently small, this can result in the log probability overflowing and giving Infinity. This can happen for multiple possible `z[i]` values, so I don't think the MCMC will be valid. One possible work-around is to avoid having nimble using the conjugate sampler for the thetas. I think this would prevent getting theta values that are so close to (or equal to) 0 and 1, but I haven't tried it. 

At a higher level, I think much of the cause of what is going on is that the model structure places density on values of alpha (and therefore elements of `ab`) near 0. This allows very extreme values of theta (very near or equal to 0 or 1). And that leads to the numerical issues. Note that a uniform distribution is the same as a Beta(1,1) or Dirichlet(1,1,...,1)). Having parameter values much less than 1 in a Beta or Dirichlet results in an unusual "u-shaped" distribution where most of the mass is near 0 and 1.

-chris

On Mon, Oct 28, 2024 at 9:35 AM Chris Paciorek <paci...@stat.berkeley.edu> wrote:
hi Brennan,

Thanks for the follow up and the additional testing.

It looks like there is another related, but distinct, numerical issue that can come up in this case. What I am seeing is that when one of the two `ab[i,1:2]` values gets close to zero, numerical underflow can cause a sampled value of `theta[i,1:2]` (from its conjugate Dirichlet distribution) to be exactly (1,0) (or (0,1)). Then if that `theta[i,1:2]` is the only member of its cluster, when the CRP sampling goes to sample a new value for `z[i]`, it's possible that the log probability density value for `theta[i,1:2]` under the other clusters are all -Inf. And using the non-conjugate CRP sampler to sample `alpha[i]` and `beta[i,1:2]` values for a new cluster will generally give values that also have -Inf for the log probability density value for `theta[i,1:2]`. At that point, the CRP sampler is trying to decide between the various possible new values for `z[i]` with all the log probabilities being -Inf and the crash occurs.

This is a tricky situation. We can of course (and will at a minimum in our upcoming release) error trap this and produce an error message rather than a crash.

However, I am not seeing a good way around the numerical problems. It's not clear to me there is a way to sample `z[i]` when `theta[i,1:2]` is (1,0) in a way that retains the validity of the MCMC sampling (i.e., I don't think sampling uniformly from the possible `z[i]` values is correct). And I don't see a reasonable way to avoid getting exact (1,0) values in the conjugate sampling of `theta[i,1:2]`.

For your case, one possible work-around (if you will generally have only two elements of theta) is that you could specify theta[i] using a beta distribution and, as needed, use truncation to ensure it never is sampled as exactly 0 or 1:

theta[i] ~ T(dbeta(ab[i,1],ab[i,2]), .001, .999)

You could also think about using the stickbreaking representation rather than the CRP.  That might avoid the issue. Or it seems that in the paper you reference, they used some other sampling strategies based on drawing from the prior.

I will try to think more about this to see if there is a better numerical solution on our end.

-chris

Hi Brennan,

It looks like this is occurring because, for the model structure and small dataset in the example, it's possible to get values in the theta and beta vectors that are exactly 0 from numerical underflow. 

The zero values in `theta` tend to happen when the `ab` values are much smaller than 1. The values of exact 0 cause the CRP sampling, which calculates the log probability density for a value of z conditional on theta, to have Infinity values when it tries to sample a new value of z, and that causes the error because we didn't anticipate the Infinity values could occur.  

The zero values in `beta` occur in the CRP sampling when attempting to create a new cluster by sampling from the prior for `beta`, and tend to happen when the `mu` values are much smaller than 1. The exact 0 value ends up causing a NaN value in the CRP sampling, which causes an error.

I'm a bit surprised this hasn't come up before, but it may be that the size of the dataset and the specific priors combine to give a somewhat unusual situation.

I've added a check that tries to handle the numerical issues more robustly, but I haven't tested it thoroughly yet.
